content: The trans effect in inorganic chemistry refers to the phenomenon where ligands positioned trans to certain other ligands become more labile, meaning they are more easily replaced or removed. These ligands are thus referred to as trans-directing ligands. The trans effect is primarily attributed to electronic effects and is most prominently observed in square planar complexes, although it can also occur in octahedral complexes. Beyond its kinetic implications, the trans effect also influences the ground state of the molecule, particularly affecting bond lengths and overall stability. Some researchers prefer to use the term trans influence to distinguish the structural or thermodynamic aspects of the effect from its kinetic manifestations. Others use more specific terms such as structural trans effect or thermodynamic trans effect. The trans effect was first identified and named by Ilya Ilich Chernyaev in 1926. Kinetic Trans Effect The strength of the trans effect, as measured by the increased rate of substitution of the trans ligand, follows a specific sequence: F⁻, H₂O, OH⁻ < NH₃ < pyridine < Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻, SCN⁻, NO₂⁻, SC(NH₂)₂, Ph⁻ < SO₃²⁻ < PR₃, AsR₃, SR₂, CH₃⁻ < H⁻, NO, CO, CN⁻, C₂H₄. A classic example of the trans effect is the synthesis of cisplatin. Starting with the PtCl₄²⁻ complex, the first NH₃ ligand can bind to any of the four equivalent positions randomly. However, the second NH₃ ligand preferentially binds cis to the first NH₃ ligand because Cl⁻ has a stronger trans effect than NH₃. Conversely, if the starting complex is Pt(NH₃)₄²⁺, the trans product is obtained instead. In square planar complexes, the trans effect can be explained by an addition/elimination mechanism that involves a trigonal bipyramidal intermediate. Ligands with a high trans effect typically exhibit high π-acidity (e.g., phosphines) or low lone pair–dπ repulsion (e.g., hydrides). These ligands preferentially occupy the more π-basic equatorial sites in the intermediate. The incoming ligand occupies the second equatorial position, and due to the principle of microscopic reversibility, the departing ligand must also leave from an equatorial position. The third equatorial site is occupied by the trans ligand. As a result, the kinetically favored product is the one where the ligand trans to the one with the largest trans effect is eliminated. Structural Trans Effect The structural trans effect can be experimentally measured using X-ray crystallography. It manifests as an elongation of the bonds between the metal center and the ligand trans to a trans-influencing ligand. For example, bond elongations of up to 2 Å are observed with strong trans-influencing ligands such as hydrides. A cis influence can also be observed, but it is generally smaller in magnitude compared to the trans influence. The relative significance of cis and trans influences depends on the formal electron configuration of the metal center. Explanations for these effects have been proposed based on the atomic orbitals involved in bonding.
